newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Sweden can't be forced into EMU - FinMin.
newsitem.headline: Sweden can't be forced into EMU - FinMin.

text.p: Swedish Finance Minister Erik Asbrink said on Wednesday Sweden could not be forced to participate in the single currency of the EMU and it was up to the Swedish parliament to decide.
"No-one can force us to join the currency union," Asbrink told an EMU debate in parliament.
Asbrink emphasised the importance of popular support on the EMU issue - a factor that has been lacking in Sweden with all opinion polls showing strong opposition to Sweden joining EMU.
"Making a decision which is in conflict with public opinion is out of the question," he said, defending the government's reluctance to take an early stance in the issue.
"The government is working to promote the conditions for a tenable decision on EMU.
"We will use the time (between now and the parliamentary decision in the autumn of 1997) to extend our knowledge of the EMU."
Asbrink maintained that Sweden now fulfills most of the Maastricht convergence criteria for monetary union, namely inflation, the budget deficit and low interest rates.
He was also optimistic with regard to the state debt.
"By 1997 we'll probably have had three years of a falling debt ratio," he said.

The finance minister repeated the Swedish government's stance that currency stability was more important than membership of Europe's Exchage Rate Mechanism (ERM) as a criterion for possible membership of the EMU.
"The ERM criterion has lost its relevance," Asbrink said, adding that the demands on Sweden's economy could become even more stringent if Sweden remains outside the currency union.
